title_en: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
title_zh: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
summary: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling t
summary_zh: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling t
body_en: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted | ANC (African National Congress)
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party .

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.
Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts , uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.
Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs .
Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

title_en: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
title_zh: Russian extremist group denies sending hoax bomb threats
summary: Scores of flights across Europe have received bomb threats this week, but no explosives have been found so far.
summary_zh: Scores of flights across Europe have received bomb threats this week, but no explosives have been found so far.
body_en: The "Male State", an extremist misogynistic group named in this week's hoax bomb threats to Italian airports, has denied any link to the false warnings causing flight disruption across Europe .

The comments to the BBC came as reports of more bomb scares to airlines began appearing, including on a Ryanair flight from Rome to Lisbon and a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome which was diverted to Venice.

Bomb threats were also reported to a number of high-profile Irish media organisations on Friday, prompting evacuations and a statement from the Irish government suggesting a "co-ordinated campaign of disruption".

Replying to the BBC Russian Service, an account on Telegram - one of several linked to the so-called "Male State" and its founder Vladislav Pozdnyakov - mocked any suggestion the group was involved in emailing the threats.

"What Male State? Where have you seen it? It hasn't existed for many years," the message on the channel reads. "If tomorrow they sign a [threat] letter, say, from Putin, will you then try to reach our president to ask your stupid question?"
The group was banned in Russia in 2021 and Pozdnyakov is now thought to live abroad. It has since renamed itself in some places as "Male Legion".
The initial hoax email, seen by the BBC, was sent on Thursday at 07:21 with the subject title: warning of a threat.

It was addressed to several offices and individuals at Aeroporti di Roma (ADR), the airport managing company in Rome, as well as accounts at the city's Fiumicino airport itself. The originating email address seems to be linked to the state health services in Bogota, Colombia.
It's not clear whether other countries' airports or airlines received the same or similar threat. At least one warning made on Friday appears to have come by phone, not email.

Written in word perfect Italian, the bizarre text sent to Rome on Thursday claimed that "fighters" of the "Male State" had planted explosives on two incoming flights in an attack on Italy's "feminist regime" that would be "remembered forever".

One flight was diverted as a result - ordered to land in France – another was escorted into Rome by Italian air force jets, scrambled for the second time this week. No explosives were found on either plane, or any other that reported receiving bomb threats.
Asked why this particular email was taken so seriously, a source at ADR in Rome told the BBC that such warnings were extremely unusual. They didn't remember anything similar in recent years.
Despite the Russian group's denial, Italy's La Stampa newspaper appears in no doubt that "Male State" was behind the threats, asking in an article whether it is acting as "the regime's armed wing".
"Attacking, and being able to deny the attacks...is part of the Russian game plan," the paper writes , external .

One Telegram channel linked to Pozdnyakov is mainly filled with virulently pro-Russian messaging about the war on Ukraine and other posts highlighting problems and tensions in Europe, including recent youth protests.
The online investigation team at Bellingcat, who studied the group back in 2022, called it then a "vocal and vile online booster" of the Russian invasion, with a clear extremist far-right ideology.

As the Europe-wide hunt continues for who is behind the spate of hoax mails, and whether they are being co-ordinated - or could be the work of copycats - Italy's defence minister has warned of a "strategy to increase chaos".
Guido Crosetto noted that he had been talking of the "hybrid threat" to Europe for some years.

"It seems to me that, day after day, from incidents involving refrigerators to the blood supply in France and now these false alarms, there are those who have an interest in fuelling tensions," the minister said on Thursday, referring to a spate of recent cyber attacks that boosted supermarket fridge temperatures, destroying mountains of produce.
"Our interest is to do the opposite and ensure the country's security," Crosetto said.

title_en: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
title_zh: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
summary: The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, says the charges are politically motivated.
summary_zh: The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, says the charges are politically motivated.
body_en: Tundu Lissu: Tanzania opposition leader found guilty of incitement but acquitted of treason - BBC News
By Wycliffe Muia and Alfred Lasteck , BBC Africa , Reporting from Dar es Salaam

Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.
A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.
But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.
Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.
The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.
"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.
Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.
"The offense of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offense that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.
He added that he would like to apply for bail as this was possible for incitement, unlike treason.
He has leave to appeal at the Court of Appeal - the country's highest court.
Treason is among Tanzania's most serious offences and can carry the death penalty.

President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote - a result the opposition dismissed the result as a "mockery" of democracy as her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded.
Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.
Tundu Lissu - the great survivor of Tanzanian politics
Demands for post-poll justice as Tanzania accused of weaponising counterterrorism laws
WATCH: Tundu Lissu: A Fight Too Far? on BBC Africa Eye's YouTube channel
The Chadema leader was arrested six months before the poll, shortly after launching a campaign demanding changes to the electoral system under the slogan "No Reforms, No Election".
Prosecutors accused him of making statements intended to incite the public to disrupt the election and threaten the government.

title_en: Rocket launcher deal illustrates deepening Russia-Iran relations
title_zh: Rocket launcher deal illustrates deepening Russia-Iran relations
summary: Report of deal comes as top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei discusses developing cooperation treaty with Putin.
summary_zh: Report of deal comes as top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei discusses developing cooperation treaty with Putin.
body_en: Share Rocket launcher deal illustrates deepening Russia-Iran relations on social media
Russia has supplied Iran with 90 advanced missile launchers, reports have said, as Moscow confirmed its close relations with Tehran.
Russia agreed a deal in 2024 to supply Iran with 90 advanced missile launchers, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing documents from a major Russian defence manufacturer.

list 2 of 3 Tech stock rout, driven by US AI fears, continues in Asian trading
list 3 of 3 Court grants ex-Malaysian PM Najib house arrest after $12m royal pardon

The report came a day after a senior Iranian official visited Moscow to discuss expanding a defence pact signed last year, and illustrates that Russia continues to deepen relations despite seeking the support of the United States for its narrative concerning the war in Ukraine.

The launchers are designed to carry Russia’s light multipurpose guided missile, known as the LMUR or Izdeliye 305. The precision weapon, capable of striking moving targets, entered military service in 2022 and has since been widely used by Russian forces in Ukraine.
The weapons are built for Russia’s Mi-28 attack helicopters, which Iran already possesses. Al Jazeera was not able to confirm if the order has been delivered.
The reported deal illustrates the strengthened military ties between Moscow and Tehran since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Western intelligence officials warn the relationship has further deepened amid the US war in the Middle East, despite President Donald Trump’s recent claims that Moscow was doing “very little, if anything” to help Iran.

The details of the deal emerged a day after Russian President Vladimir Putin met top Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei at the Kremlin. Rezaei delivered a message from Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during the visit, which was aimed at “further development of bilateral cooperation”, the Kremlin said in a statement released on Friday.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met with Putin in late October.
The two countries, both under heavy Western sanctions, have continued to pull closer together in recent years.
In January 2025, they signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty covering trade, military cooperation, science, culture, and education.
The treaty took effect in October of that year, but unlike Russia’s pact with North Korea, it does not include a mutual defence clause.

However, the deal to supply the helicopter-mounted launchers highlights that military ties continue to strengthen. On Saturday, Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Tehran had bought Russian Su-35 fighter jets.

Meanwhile, amid the war in Ukraine, Tehran has provided Moscow with ammunition, artillery shells, firearms, short-range ballistic missiles, helmets, and flak jackets. It was suspected to be supplying drones.

After meeting Putin on Thursday, Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said the talks had focused on security arrangements in the region, as well as Russia’s support for ending what he called the US “aggression” against Iran.
“Important regional issues were discussed with Putin and significant conversations took place regarding the post-war period and regional security arrangements,” Rezaei said.

title_en: Low pressure in US midwest brings unseasonable heat to New York and Boston
title_zh: Low pressure in US midwest brings unseasonable heat to New York and Boston
summary: Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in
summary_zh: Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in
body_en: Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado

Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in recent days. Temperatures approached 23C (73F) in New York and Boston, about 7-10C above what is expected in early November. The unseasonable warmth spilled into parts of eastern Canada, with temperatures exceeding 20C, about 10-15C above normal for the time of year. The balmy conditions were caused by an area of low pressure in the US midwest, dragging up exceptionally warm air from the Gulf of Mexico along its eastern flank. This area of low pressure will gradually drift eastwards, allowing temperatures to fall closer to the average.

Further south, severe thunderstorms have resulted in numerous flood warnings and evacuation warnings being issued this week across many states, with disruptive weather affecting polling stations in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado. The powerful thunderstorms even resulted in a tornado touching down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forcing the relocation of a polling station. The tornado caused extensive damage, although no causalities have been reported. Officials across many states have requested federal funding assistance after the extreme weather resulted in widespread damage to homes and infrastructure.

title_en: Global stocks plunge amid AI slowdown fears after Democrats’ midterm triumph
title_zh: Global stocks plunge amid AI slowdown fears after Democrats’ midterm triumph
summary: Asian and European markets follow Wall Street with sharp fall as FTSE down 1.9% Business live – latest updates European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fear
summary_zh: Asian and European markets follow Wall Street with sharp fall as FTSE down 1.9% Business live – latest updates European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fear
body_en: Asian and European markets follow Wall Street with sharp fall as FTSE down 1.9%
European stock markets have fallen sharply as a rout in US tech stocks spread across the Atlantic, after the Democrats’ midterms victory sparked fears of a slowdown in the AI industry.

A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stocks markets on Friday morning. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market is poised for its worst day since March.
The FTSE 100 index, which tracks blue-chip shares listed in London, was down 207 points, or 1.9%, at 10,575 points in mid-morning trading.
Germany’s Dax index fell by 1.9% in morning trading, France’s Cac 40 dropped by 1.5% and Spain’s Ibex lost 1.1%.

Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe .

“Big worries are colliding – the build-out of datacentres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment.”
On Thursday the Nasdaq share index had its worst day in 19 months after slumping 5.5%.

Chip stocks led the slump, with the memory maker SanDisk tumbling by 22% and the hard drive maker Western Digital falling by 17%. Wall Street’s “fear index”, the Vix, jumped by 61% to its highest levels since the early weeks of the Iran war, in a sign of rising market volatility.
The heavy falls continued in Asia on Friday, with Japan’s Nikkei 225 index sinking 6% and South Korea’s Kospi index tumbling more than 8%.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, the head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets. “[Clients] were long index, long stocks, and they all got carried out. All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome, and you’re telling them: ‘Look, you’ve just lost money.’”

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “Yesterday’s brutal session marked a dramatic turnaround from Wednesday, but with AI fears still prominent there is a risk that there is much more selling to come.

“Investors remain on watch for a potential resumption of the Iran conflict, and are nervously watching the oil price after its slump earlier in the week. All in all it remains a very febrile atmosphere.”
However, despite the sharp losses suffered on global stock markets around the world, most indices are still up for the year.
The Nasdaq Composite index remains up 4.6% since the start of January – even though it is more than 10% below its peak.
The FTSE 100 has gained almost 6.9% in 2026 – but it is now more than 300 points below the record high set in July.

Mohit Kumar, an economist at the investment bank Jefferies, said that while he did not expect a quick rebound from Thursday’s losses in the US, he also did not believe it marked the “start of the unwind of the AI trade”.

He said: “AI investment has been a key driver of US growth and we do not see the Democrats as giving up on this growth engine. Datacentres and AI infrastructure also create jobs and Democrats would be reluctant to let those jobs move on to other states or outside the country.”
Stock market tremors have also hit the London Metal Exchange, with copper set for its biggest weekly fall since March.

title_en: White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses
title_zh: White House denies Hegseth and Rubio to leave jobs after Republican election losses
summary: US media reports there are calls to replace Pete Hegseth, who also faces a possible impeachment vote, while Marco Rubio is rumoured to be eyeing a presidential run.
summary_zh: US media reports there are calls to replace Pete Hegseth, who also faces a possible impeachment vote, while Marco Rubio is rumoured to be eyeing a presidential run.
body_en: The White House has denied rumours that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio might leave their jobs in a post-election shakeup of the Trump administration.
US media have reported there are calls to replace Hegseth - in particular over his handling of the Iran war, which is being blamed for heavy Republican election losses.

One outgoing congressional Republican has threatened to force an impeachment vote against Hegseth as early as next week. The defence secretary posted a video statement defending his record and denouncing the effort.
"You see, they attack me. They attack us because we are effective," he said. "It's not going to work. We will not back down."
Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
Meanwhile, Rubio is denying reports he is considering leaving his post ahead of a 2028 presidential run.
Working for Trump until the end of his term has "always been my plan," Rubio told The New York Times in an interview.
"I love the work I'm doing," Rubio said. "And plus I always laugh when they say he's going to leave his job. I go, 'Which one?'"
The White House and US State Department also shut down reports that Rubio might be leaving after this week's midterm losses, with both calling it "fake news".
The defence secretary, though, faces a more uncertain political future.
Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have both blamed the Iran war for Republican losses that allowed Democrats full control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
In a telephone interview with ABC News, Trump said that he had received "calls about" Hegseth, but added that he had "every intention" of keeping him.

Later on Thursday, he told reporters at the White House that "Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job", and went on to list what he sees are some of his achievements, including the arrest of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in January and the Iran war, now into its ninth month.

The Washington Post reported on Thursday that Trump might be, however, considering ousting General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, or Centcom chief Admiral Brad Cooper. Both played significant roles in offering guidance on the war, which started eight months ago.
Meanwhile, Republican Representative Thomas Massie, a frequent critic of Trump, has said he will push ahead with plans to push for Hegseth's impeachment.
He told news site Politico that he will trigger his resolution to impeach the defence secretary early next week.

title_en: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
title_zh: Kenyan doomsday cult leader given life sentence for murdering 191 people
summary: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".
summary_zh: Paul Mackenzie ordered his followers to starve their children to death in a forest so they could "meet Jesus".
body_en: Shakahola deaths: Kenya court doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie sentenced to 200 years in prison - BBC News
By Basillioh Rukanga and Wycliffe Muia , Reporting from Nairobi
A Kenyan court has sentenced the leader of a doomsday cult, Paul Mackenzie, to 200 years in prison for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children.
Alongside 28 others, Mackenzie was found guilty of the murders for instructing members of his cult to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus".
Justice Diana Mochache said Mackenzie bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering his followers to fast to death, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.
"The sentence is appropriate and just, to send an unmistakable message that such atrocities warrant the maximum penalties allowed by law," the judge added.

The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. The sprawling investigation into the cases shocked Kenya and drew international attention.
The court sentenced Mackenzie to 100 years in prison for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation.
The sentences within each category will run concurrently, but the two sets will run consecutively, bringing his total prison term to 200 years.
Mackenzie also faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.
Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, arguing that the scale and circumstances of the killings warranted the harshest punishment.
However, Justice Mochache declined to impose the death penalty, despite ruling that the case met the threshold for its consideration.

"Nevertheless, the court declines the invitation to impose the death penalty on any of the victims," she said, adding that capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation and disengagement. The death sentence has not been carried out in Kenya since 1987.
Mackenzie was tried alongside 28 accomplices, including guards who enforced his fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal the victims' bodies in mass graves.
They received varying prison sentences of up to 160 years.
Justice Mochache described the killings as "cold and calculated", saying the perpetrators had shown no remorse and had even declared their willingness to fast to death themselves.

Before the hearing began on Friday morning, Francis Wanje, who lost eight relatives including two grandchildren in Shakahola forest, told the BBC's Newsday programme that he was "hoping for... a sentence which will match his [Mackenzie's] deeds in the forest".
Mackenzie and the co-accused had asked for leniency from the court.
Before their conviction on 19 October, they had all pleaded not guilty and repeatedly insisted that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's followers believed he was "Jesus's mouthpiece", Justice Mochache said as she delivered her eight-hour judgement last month.

title_en: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
title_zh: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
summary: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.
summary_zh: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.
body_en: One child and one young adult have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.
The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent, around 34 miles (55km) from the border with Switzerland.
The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".
The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and a further 13 have sustained minor injuries.
A young girl and an 18-year-old man have been identified as the two who died in the incident by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.
The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries".
The driver has been taken to hospital after sustaining injuries and has not yet been questioned by police, the prosecutor's office added.
Photos circulating in French media show a blue and white bus tilted in what appears to be a ditch on the roadside. Trees line the side of the road. The front of the bus appears to be heavily damaged.
Local mayor Cristin told BFM TV: "I arrived minutes after the accident and people were in shock.
"The side of the bus was torn off, and clearly, the people who were on that side must have been seriously injured."
Addressing weather conditions at the time of the crash, the mayor told Le Figaro "there was a bit of fog, the road was wet" but there were "no major difficulties".
Speaking to the same paper, Fabrice Pannekoucke, head of the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region, said: "At this stage, there are no particular explanations or interpretations that can be given."
French Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said the bus did not operate "exclusively on school routes" but that there were "many schoolchildren on board".
Earlier, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said it was "always difficult when our children are victims of accidents of this nature".
Emergency services were at the scene and medical helicopters were deployed to take victims with serious injuries to a specialised hospital.
More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes were also at the scene.
The local town hall was opened to provide shelter and coordinate with emergency services, the local mayor said.

title_en: Pope begins lengthy trip to Latin America weeks after lung cancer surgery
title_zh: 肺癌手术几周后，教皇开始了漫长的拉丁美洲之行
summary: Pope Leo, who had part of a lung removed last month, will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
summary_zh: 上个月切除了部分肺部的教皇利奥将访问乌拉圭、阿根廷和秘鲁。
body_en: Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent, Rome

Pope Leo XIV is beginning a lengthy trip to Latin America just three weeks after surgery for lung cancer - a tour that includes a much-anticipated "homecoming" to Peru where he was a priest for many years.

The Vatican says no extraordinary measures are being taken in relation to the Pope's health, describing him as a "71-year-old who has undergone an operation" not someone with a "permanent medical condition".

It was Leo himself who revealed last month that doctors had discovered a tumour during a routine scan. The growth was removed along with the lower lobe of his right lung and his medical team then confirmed the cancer had not spread.

At a briefing in Rome ahead of the trip, which takes in Uruguay and Argentina as well as Peru, a spokeswoman stressed that Pope Leo had "fantastic stamina" and was "extremely enthusiastic" about the schedule which he had "personally confirmed... with no changes".

"The Vatican's message with this trip is, 'that was a short episode and now we're back on track'," Professor Massimo Faggioli of Villanova University told the BBC, pointing out that the Pope has had a busy return to work since his surgery.
"We have seen him in these last few days making speeches, audiences and so on. He seems in great shape. That was important."
The 12-day tour would be demanding for anyone, though. It incorporates multiple long-haul and local flights and covers thousands of miles from the Amazon to the Andes.
The starting point will be Uruguay, where the number of Catholics has fallen away steeply in recent years and which is getting its first Papal visit in four decades.
Leo then heads for Argentina, homeland of Pope Francis, his predecessor.
"This visit is also a homage to Francis, who didn't make it to Argentina [as pope]," says Father Fernando Laguna, the rector of Santa Maria Addolorata, Argentina's national church in Rome.

"When this visit by Pope Leo was announced, it filled all of our hearts with joy," he told the BBC. "I always thought he would go, despite his illness. I don't think he ever thought of calling it off!"

The priest is installing a big screen inside the church in Rome to allow parishioners to follow all the key moments of the trip from afar. The building is already decked out with posters declaring Pope Leo is welcome in Argentina. "We're waiting for you!", one proclaims.

This leg of the Pope's journey - which includes meetings with heads of state as well as religious events - could be the most politically sensitive. President Javier Milei once called Pope Francis "evil on earth" and a "communist" for promoting a doctrine of social justice to help the poor. In turn, Argentina's bishops have criticised Milei's harsh austerity measures, making sweeping cuts to social spending.
But Milei has already welcomed Pope Leo, writing in a post on X that Argentina awaits "with immense joy". Millions are expected to turn out to greet him.
The highlight of the trip is undoubtedly saved for last, when Pope Leo reaches Peru - described by the Vatican as a return to his roots.
"He knows these streets," is how a spokeswoman put it.
Born in the US, the then Robert Prevost spent almost 20 years in Peru, on and off, and even has Peruvian citizenship. That time is seen as fundamental to shaping his papacy.
His schedule includes a return to the diocese of Chiclayo where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until Francis moved him to the Vatican almost a decade later.
He will also travel to Cusco, former capital of the Inca Empire, to say Mass more than 3,000m above sea level before heading to Pucallpa in the Amazon.
body_zh: 南欧和东欧记者，罗马
教皇利奥十四世在肺癌手术后仅三周，就开始了对拉丁美洲的漫长访问，其中包括万众期待的“返乡”秘鲁，他在那里担任了多年的牧师。
梵蒂冈表示，没有针对教皇的健康采取任何特别措施，称他是一名“接受过手术的71岁老人”，而不是患有“永久性健康状况”的人。
利奥本人上个月透露，医生在例行扫描中发现了肿瘤。肿瘤连同他的右肺下叶一起被切除，他的医疗团队随后证实癌症没有扩散。
此次行程将访问乌拉圭、阿根廷和秘鲁，在罗马举行的新闻发布会上，一位女发言人强调，教皇利奥拥有“惊人的耐力”，并对他“亲自确认的行程……没有任何改变”感到“非常热情”。
维拉诺瓦大学的马西莫·法吉奥利教授告诉英国广播公司：“梵蒂冈此次访问传达的信息是，‘那是一个短暂的插曲，现在我们又回到了正轨’。”他指出，教皇手术后返回工作岗位一直很忙碌。
“过去几天我们看到他发表演讲、观众等等。他看起来状态很好。这很重要。”
不过，12 天的旅程对任何人来说都是艰巨的。它包含多个长途和本地航班，覆盖从亚马逊到安第斯山脉的数千英里。
起点将是乌拉圭，该国的天主教徒人数近年来急剧下降，而教皇四十年来首次访问该国。
随后，利奥前往前任教皇方济各的祖国阿根廷。
“这次访问也是对方济各的致敬，他没有以教皇身份来到阿根廷，”位于罗马的阿根廷国家教堂圣玛丽亚阿多洛拉塔教堂的教区费尔南多·拉古纳神父说。
他告诉英国广播公司：“当利奥教皇此次访问的消息被宣布时，我们所有人的心中都充满了喜悦。” “尽管他生病了，但我一直以为他会去。我认为他从来没有想过取消！”
神父正在罗马教堂内安装一个大屏幕，让教区居民可以从远处观看旅途中的所有关键时刻。这座建筑已经贴满了海报，宣布教皇利奥在阿根廷受到欢迎。 “我们在等你！”，其中一人宣称。
教皇旅程的这一阶段——包括与国家元首的会面以及宗教活动——可能是政治上最敏感的。哈维尔·米莱总统曾称教皇方济各是“地球上的邪恶”和“共产主义者”，因为他提倡帮助穷人的社会正义学说。反过来，阿根廷主教们批评了米莱严厉的紧缩措施，大幅削减了社会支出。
但米雷已经欢迎了教皇利奥，她在 X 上的一篇帖子中写道，阿根廷“怀着巨大的喜悦”等待着。预计将有数百万人前来迎接他。
这次旅行的亮点无疑被留到了最后，即教皇利奥抵达秘鲁——梵蒂冈称其为回归根源。
“他熟悉这些街道，”一位发言人说道。
出生于美国的罗伯特·普雷沃斯特断断续续地在秘鲁度过了近20年，甚至拥有秘鲁公民身份。那段时间被视为塑造他的教皇职位的基础。
他的日程安排包括返回奇克拉约教区，并于 2014 年被任命为主教，直到近十年后方济各将他调往梵蒂冈。
他还将前往印加帝国前首都库斯科，在海拔3000m以上的地方做弥撒，然后前往亚马逊地区的普卡尔帕。

title_en: Born to be torn: A generation raised under Houthi rule in Yemen
title_zh: Born to be torn: A generation raised under Houthi rule in Yemen
summary: As children are recruited to fight, the cost of failing to confront the Houthis is being felt far beyond Yemen.
summary_zh: As children are recruited to fight, the cost of failing to confront the Houthis is being felt far beyond Yemen.
body_en: Founder and President of Yafa American Community Center.
Share Born to be torn: A generation raised under Houthi rule in Yemen on social media

Nearly eight years ago, I warned about a generation of Yemeni children growing up under Houthi rule. At a time when some were still hoping that people in Saada, northern Yemen, would rise against the group, I questioned what would become of an entire generation raised under its control.

Today, that warning carries a devastating weight. Children born under Houthi rule are now being recruited to fight. Schools and summer camps have been used for indoctrination and military training, exposing young people to recruitment when they should be receiving an education and building a future. These practices were documented by the United Nations Panel of Experts on Yemen and the US Department of Labor.

A childhood consumed by fear cannot simply be restored when the guns fall silent. The damage reaches into education, livelihoods, relationships, and the ability to imagine a life beyond war. UNICEF describes the profound effects of disrupted schooling on children’s learning, emotional development, and mental health.

This is why waiting for an uprising against the Houthis has never been a sufficient strategy. People living under coercion face consequences that distant observers do not. Silence under repression cannot be treated as consent, nor can survival be mistaken for allegiance.

But the consequences of allowing Houthi power to grow extend far beyond the people living under its control. The recent attacks across Aden, Hadramout, Shabwa, and Saudi Arabia show how urgently international policy must confront this threat.

In Aden, the October 15 attack on Maashiq Palace brought explosions and renewed fear to the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government. A subsequent reported attack on Aden’s airport on October 21 further underscored the vulnerability of a city whose residents need dependable access to transport and essential services.

For the people of Aden, renewed bombardment carries the memory of earlier battles alongside the anxiety of what comes next. A population struggling to rebuild should not repeatedly be forced to organise daily life around the possibility of another missile.

In Hadramout, reports on October 21 described strikes on Al-Rayyan International Airport in Mukalla, with no injuries initially reported. The AFP news agency also reported that a military base at the airport was hit. The presence of military facilities does not diminish the importance of protecting civilians and the infrastructure on which they depend. Airports connect people to medical treatment, employment, relatives, and the outside world.

In Shabwa, the October 19 missile attack hit the Al-Alam training camp for security forces, causing mass casualties. The Reuters news agency reported dozens killed and more than 200 injured, citing the governor. The strike dealt a devastating blow to personnel responsible for maintaining local security, with losses felt far beyond the camp, in the communities mourning their dead and caring for the wounded.

Across the border, attacks on Saudi airports have killed civilians and disrupted international travel. The October 10 strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people. Travellers of different nationalities have been exposed to a conflict they did not choose. The danger already extends beyond Yemen’s borders.

Together, these attacks reveal the failure of an approach that has not sufficiently constrained Houthi capabilities. Diplomatic activity cannot be measured by meetings held or assurances received while missiles continue to reach cities, airports, and vital infrastructure.

The record also demands clarity about the Houthis’ terrorist designations. Yemen’s National Defence Council designated the group a terrorist organisation in October 2022, and the United States designated it a Foreign Terrorist Organization, effective March 5, 2025. In my judgement, their documented conduct amply warrants those decisions.

Other governments should take those designations and the evidence behind them seriously. Engagement must carry conditions, verification, and consequences. The Houthis signed a UN action plan in April 2022 to end grave violations against children, including recruitment. Subsequent reporting by Human Rights Watch documented continued child recruitment. Commitments must therefore be judged by their implementation, not merely by the signing of documents.

Token penalties or political rewards for terrorism would set a dangerous precedent in international relations: Violence wins concessions, and armed coercion buys political power. Other armed groups could draw the same lesson, potentially including groups closer to home for the countries failing to act.

A credible response must disrupt illicit weapons supplies and financing, strengthen civilian protection, defend maritime navigation, and impose targeted consequences on those directing and enabling abuses. Humanitarian assistance and legitimate commerce must remain protected. Civilians should never pay twice: First for Houthi repression, then for measures intended to confront it.

Protecting the next generation also requires sustained investment in education, independent information, psychosocial care, and the reintegration of children released from armed groups. UNICEF’s child protection work in Yemen includes psychosocial support and reintegration assistance. Preventing recruitment means giving children and their communities a viable future.

North and South Yemen face immediate dangers, and Saudi Arabia and international shipping have already felt the consequences. No government should assume that a threat left to grow will remain geographically contained.
Nearly eight years after my warning, another generation cannot be asked to wait. The threat is established. International policy must finally match it.

title_en: "No choice but to bear it": Delhi's unrelenting air pollution crisis
title_zh: "No choice but to bear it": Delhi's unrelenting air pollution crisis
summary: Despite years of government interventions, emergency restrictions and public outrage, Delhi continues to battle dangerously polluted air every winter. Why isn't there a lasting solution to a predictable crisis?
summary_zh: Despite years of government interventions, emergency restrictions and public outrage, Delhi continues to battle dangerously polluted air every winter. Why isn't there a lasting solution to a predictable crisis?
body_en: On a slightly chilly and distinctly smoggy morning in New Delhi, Khushboo Arora was looking for another air purifier for her mother, who has underlying health complications, before the city's air quality deteriorated further.

"Already, I am starting to get a recurring headache," she said. "These days when I wake up, I don't feel fresh. As the day progresses, I feel a heaviness in my head, itching in my eye and a constantly parched throat."
Not too long ago, the unpacking of woolens announced the advent of winter in Delhi. Now, it's the light hum of an air purifier in the corner.

Arora said she has already stopped doing yoga in the park and taking her morning walks. She has also filled her house with air-purifying plants and started spraying water mist inside the house to bring down the level of pollution .
"My parents look at me like I have gone mad. But I feel people are not realizing the gravity of the situation," she said.

Winters in Delhi increasingly follow a familiar pattern: Air quality deteriorates, residents struggle to breathe, emergency restrictions kick in and governments exchange blame. Then the season changes, only for the cycle to repeat the following year.

On Thursday, Delhi's air fell into the "Very unhealthy" category, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir, with an average PM2.5 concentration of 157.9 micrograms per cubic meter of air. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends an annual safe limit of no more than 5 micrograms.

Studies have shown that exposure to PM2.5 — air particles with a diameter smaller than 2.5 micrometers that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream — is associated with an increased incidence of head and neck cancer (HNC), like oral, nasal and throat cancers.
But despite years of attempted interventions, India 's capital continues to struggle with the same pollution crisis.
Delhi is not dealing with an unknown problem. There is considerable scientific understanding of its causes.

A 2026 assessment by an expert panel reviewed by the Delhi government identified the major winter contributors of PM2.5 as vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road and construction dust, biomass and waste burning, and pollution from neighboring regions.

Sunil Dahiya, founder of the environmental group EnviroCatalysts, said Delhi is part of a larger airshed. On most winter days, more pollution comes into Delhi than is generated inside it, according to the environmentalist.

"Analysis of the government's Decision Support System (DSS) data for winter 2025 found that around 65% of Delhi's PM2.5 came from outside the city and about 35% from sources within it," he told DW, adding that neighboring Noida and Gurugram, which comprise the National Capital Region (NCR), are some of the biggest contributors.
Coordinating action across the NCR, which spans Delhi and parts of three neighboring states, remains a major obstacle.
"This is a shared problem, and no single city can solve it alone," Dahiya said.
To understand why existing policies have not delivered sustained improvements , Dahiya highlighted the gap between scientific recommendations and state action.
"Scientists have said for over a decade that we need airshed-wide, year-round, source-specific action. What we mostly get is seasonal and reactive," he said.

According to the environmentalist, emergency restrictions kick in only after pollution has reached dangerous levels. Short-term measures such as water sprinklers and smog towers provide little relief, while bigger structural changes are slow to materialize. These include stricter enforcement of industrial emissions, cleaner fuels, expanded public transport, vehicle electrification and viable alternatives to crop burning for farmers.

"The science is not the bottleneck. Implementation, regional coordination and political will are," said Dahiya. "Until targets are tied to emission reductions at each source, and someone is held accountable for meeting them, we will keep having the same conversation every November."
Bhavreen Kandhari, co-founder of Warrior Moms, agrees that official responses focus on reacting rather than preventing.

title_en: Nigerian court rules opposition candidate cannot stand in elections
title_zh: Nigerian court rules opposition candidate cannot stand in elections
summary: The high court has sacked the leadership of the opposition ADC party with only months to go until elections.
summary_zh: The high court has sacked the leadership of the opposition ADC party with only months to go until elections.
body_en: Will Nigeria's Atiku Abubakar be on the presidential ballot after ADC court ruling? - BBC News
By Mansur Abubakar , Reporting from Abuja and Lucy Fleming

Nigeria's Federal High Court has sacked the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress (ADC) party - and also ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid.
A statement from the ADC said the ruling was another desperate attempt to cripple the opposition.
Presidential elections are scheduled to take place on 16 January when President Bola Tinubu's main challengers are again expected to be Abubakar and former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi.
Several high-profile politicians joined the ADC in 2025 - disillusioned by the factional infighting in the once powerful Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).
Among them were Abubakar - who had served as vice-president between 1999 and 2007 when the PDP was in power - and former Senate president David Mark.
As accommodations were made for the line-up of political heavyweights, Mark took over as its interim chairman.
But Nafiu Bala Gombe, a former ADC national deputy chairman, argued before the court that this was not lawful as Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention.
Instead, he said, he himself should have taken over the party's leadership following the resignation of the ADC's former chairman in 2025.
This is not first time the Federal High Court in the capital, Abuja, has ruled on the leadership of the party.
In July, judge Musa Liman said Mark had been chosen in accordance with the country's laws and the party's constitution - in a case brought by another former ADC member.
Abubakar said the latest case raised serious legal concerns: "Why, after that judgment, was another case filed to reopen the same dispute?"

In a statement, the ADC added that Thursday's judgement by Justice Peter Lifu was aimed at stifling the opposition momentum and "was a calculated attempt to weaken the ADC and frustrate" Abubakar's candidacy.
The ADC says it will challenge the ruling at the Court of Appeal.
In a statement on X, Abubakar, 79, said it showed the "panic was real" by those who felt threatened by his candidacy , external .
He said the timing of the judgment was telling as it came "barely a day after a mammoth crowd turned out in Sokoto [northern Nigeria] to welcome him" at the launch of his campaign.
"The people of Sokoto came out in their thousands because they are hungry for change and believe in our promise to make life affordable again. What we witnessed in Sokoto is only the beginning."
Political parties in Nigeria have increasingly been taking internal issues to court.

But as it stands, the electoral commission has issued its final list of candidates , external - and Abubakar is on the ticket for the ADC with former Rivers State Governor Rotimi Amaechi as his running mate.

title_en: ‘Nobody can stop them’: Who are Europe’s Black Bloc protesters?
title_zh: ‘Nobody can stop them’: Who are Europe’s Black Bloc protesters?
summary: Anarchistic activists who dress in black and clash with police are a regular feature of protests from France to Albania.
summary_zh: Anarchistic activists who dress in black and clash with police are a regular feature of protests from France to Albania.
body_en: Share ‘Nobody can stop them’: Who are Europe’s Black Bloc protesters? on social media

From France and Italy to Spain and Albania, a regular feature of European protest movements has been the presence of a few hundred young people fully dressed in black, often engaged in physical violence with law enforcement.
They have been seen smashing public and private property and setting fire to cars and buildings, and are accused of break-ins and stealing consumer goods – anything from food to jewellery.
list of 4 items list 1 of 4 ‘What’s wrong with citizens taking to the streets with a Palestinian flag?’
list 2 of 4 Why are Europe’s governments struggling to respond to growing protests?
list 3 of 4 Danish students join European protest wave against education funding cuts
list 4 of 4 Hundreds of thousands protest across France over high cost of living

Known as the “Black Bloc”, they have aggressive energy that can upend otherwise peaceful demonstrations by student groups and professional unions. While some say they bring attention to social, political, and economic inequalities, others condemn their violent methods, saying they distract from protesters’ legitimate demands.

“The movement started in the 1980s in Germany and came from a social movement called autonomia, or autonomy,” political science professor Francis Dupuis-Deri, at the University of Quebec in Montreal, told Al Jazeera. “They were against the state, capitalism, political parties, even communists and unions. They were more or less anarchists. They believe in living outside the system.”
Dupuis-Deri, who has authored a book on Black Blocs, explained that the anarchists’ idea was “simple”.

“You wear black suits, which was a punk fashion at the time, black leather jackets and cotton hoodies, motorcycle helmets, sunglasses and bandanas. This was a way of making sure they could not be recognised by the police … There is no leadership, no hierarchy, no superstars, no spokesperson, no press statements,” he said.

But he warned against associating the group with any political ideology, left or right, as there have been episodes of right-wing nationalist and neo-Nazi groups in Poland and Germany using Black Bloc attire and violent tactics, although not in recent years.
France has for weeks seen mass student and union demonstrations and is grappling with a high level of violence and property damage.

Al Jazeera contacted the office of a left-wing French member of the European Parliament (MEP), whose party has organised and supported recent nationwide rallies, about the black-clad protesters. But they said the issue was too sensitive to discuss.

“A few cases of violence are used by the government to criminalise our movement and our party, so we don’t want to enter the strategy of speaking about it,” said a person who was not authorised to speak officially on behalf of his elected official.
Italy has also witnessed violence in Rome, Milan, and Turin, with people clashing with police, setting bins and cars on fire, and in some cases causing extensive property damage and injuries.

“Frankly, I’m not aware of any movement inspired by the Black Blocs,” said Mario Furore, an Italian member of the European Parliament from the Five Star Movement. “In Milan, there have been incidents of looting and vandalism, and those responsible appear to have been very young, many of them minors.

“To me, this looks more like copycat behaviour and the influence of bad role models than the work of an organised network. However, it will be up to the judicial authorities investigating the incidents to establish the facts.”

The Black Bloc is not a homogeneous or organised movement with any known leadership or structure. It is also politically somewhat irrelevant because governments and law enforcement groups associate the groups with social protests, whether they are “copycats” or genuine.

Dupuis-Deri said the lack of organisational structure allows members to find each other quickly based on their attire, but they also congregate through word of mouth and form relationships over several demonstrations.

summary_zh: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday, November 8, whom he will task with trying to form a new government, following post-election talks with all party leaders. 46 parliament members recommended Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while
body_en: Israeli President Isaac Herzog said he will announce on Sunday, November 8, whom he will task with trying to form a new government, following post-election talks with all party leaders. 46 parliament members recommended Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while 67 backed his opponent Gadi Eisenkot. title_en: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
title_zh: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
summary: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.
summary_zh: Musk said it was to make room for production of its Cybercabs - autonomous taxis without a driver.
body_en: Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.
He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."
With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.
Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it " the best vehicle Tesla has ever made , external " as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".
Musk responded to the user , external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was " way more awesome than people realise , external " in March, and called it the " best product Tesla has ever made to date , external " in April.
But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.
It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.
Despite the gaffe, the Cybertruck ended up receiving a 146,000 orders, Musk said in 2019 , while it was still in development.
In the end, the vehicle launched in 2023, keeping its novel design - an angular shape with a body made of stainless steel.
Tesla fans praised its retro-futuristic look, which some said looked like something " straight out of Blade Runner , external ".
But critics were far less kind, joking about its appearance and labelling it " ugly as sin , external ".
Several recalls - including in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 Cybertrucks over concerns part of its trim could fall off - would not have helped.
"We need to make it at a price that people can afford," Musk told Wall Street analysts that year - which ended up being $61,000 (then £48,000) for all the "bells and whistles".
In 2026, the so-called "Cyberbeast" model comes in at $102,000.

Tesla truck has 150,000 orders despite launch gaffe

title_en: Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument
title_zh: Trump signs order to preserve Oval Office as national monument
summary: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
summary_zh: The order comes after Trump made a series of big changes to the decor of the Oval Office and tore down the White House East Wing.
body_en: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order that he says will prevent future presidents from making certain changes to the White House Oval Office.
The executive order declares the president's official office, which he has renovated, to be a national monument.

"We're making it a national monument, and it will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Trump told reporters on Thursday.
The order does not prevent future presidents from changing the decor of the famous room.

The document says that it does not "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character".
American presidents currently have the power to make some changes to the White House but large projects require the permission of Congress.
The order comes months after Trump tore down the entirety of the White House East Wing in a project that has faced legal challenges.
The project was not approved by the US Congress. Construction has continued, with plans to turn the space into a new ballroom.
How Trump is remaking the White House in his own image

Signing the new executive order on Thursday, the president said: "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself. It's a symbol of our country and the greatness of our country."
He added that world leaders who have visited in recent months have complimented his decorative changes to the room.
Trump said the White House and the Oval Office had been in need of repairs before his changes, calling it "badly damaged". He described broken windows, cracked walls and broken stone.
Many of the noticeable changes, though, were cosmetic, including a large gold plaque reading "Oval Office" outside the space, paving over the Rose Garden and adding a new helicopter pad.
Trump said the order would "make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space".
It is unclear whether this action could simply be reversed by a future president or a legal challenge.
Most executive orders can be overturned and Trump himself scaled back two national monuments in Utah in 2017. But revoking a national monument designation has not yet been tested in court.
The White House grounds are already designated as a National Historic Landmark, which is intended to prevent against sudden changes to the building.
Trump's order calls on the Oval Office to be maintained by the National Park Service "in a manner that protects its historic character, architectural integrity, and association with the Presidency".

It notes the existing protections to the White House, but says "nonetheless, the Oval Office merits specific recognition and protective management as a discrete historic structure of national significance".

Congress has carved out an exemption to the National Historic Preservation Act, in order to allow presidents to make needed changes. The current Oval Office has existed since the early 1930s, after its conception by President Franklin D Roosevelt.

title_en: Americans voted against Trump's Iran war. Gulf countries hope that means an end to the conflict
title_zh: 美国人投票反对特朗普的伊朗战争。海湾国家希望这意味着冲突的结束
summary: The US midterm results showed how unpopular Donald Trump's Iran war is. Now, Gulf countries, trapped for months in the middle of the war between the US and Iran, see reason for optimism.
summary_zh: 美国中期选举结果显示，唐纳德·特朗普的伊朗战争是多么不受欢迎。现在，海湾国家被困在美国之间的战争中数月之久。
body_en: After his party's resounding defeat in the US midterm elections this week, President Donald Trump conceded that the war with Iran had likely played a part.

"I think a part of it was Iran, but, at the same time, people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump told Fox News, conceding that US voters were unwilling to accept the impact of the war on gas prices.
Observers say the United States and Israel had been holding off on major attacks on Iran until after both had held elections .
At the end of October, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Trump administration was already warning Gulf state governments to brace for a short, intense military campaign after the midterms.

While foreign policy is a US president's purview, analysts have pointed out that a Congress controlled by the Democratic party could ostensibly withhold funding for Trump's military expeditions. However newly-elected Democratic politicians won't take their seats until early next year.

As two US professors of political science wrote for Foreign Affairs magazine this week, past American presidents, like Trump, who become "lame ducks" — that is, a president who loses control of Congress and can't run for another term — have often ramped up international interventions.

"As they think about their legacy, lame ducks often turn to foreign policy, where the power of the presidency allows them to act unfettered by pesky domestic politics," they explained. And one of the places where Trump is most likely to act is Iran , the professors argued.
On the other hand, Trump also told several media outlets that he was in "no rush" to start bombing Iran again .
Opinions on Iran's next moves are also divided.

The Iranians have said they're ready for any attack and rhetoric from senior leaders indicates they may be willing to strike a wider range of targets than previously. That could include regional energy and economic infrastructure and even undersea telecommunications cabling or data centers.

If Iran thinks there is an existential threat to its leadership, then "all bets are off," Ross Harrison, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Middle East Institute, or MEI, and an expert on Iran, said during a virtual briefing hosted by MEI this week. "I think they will target differently in the Gulf states [this time] … so it really depends on how all this unfolds."
But other experts believe Iran was deliberately holding out to pressure Trump before the midterms. Now the election is over , the Iranians may be more willing to negotiate a peace deal.
All this leaves the Gulf states, who have been the main targets of Iranian attacks since the conflict began, in a difficult position.

"We find ourselves drawn within a crisis that we worked diplomatically very hard to try to avert," Anwar Gargash, a foreign policy adviser to United Arab Emirates leadership, said at a security conference in Bahrain last weekend, the Manama Dialogue hosted by the International Institute for Strategic Studies, or IISS. "We are clearly seeking a political off-ramp."

Qatar has been trying to negotiate between the US and Iran but has also been conducting emergency drills at its airport. The Emiratis have been doing similar drills. And Saudi Arabia is looking at a war on two fronts: The oil-rich state is already under attack from the Houthi militia in neighboring Yemen . Even Egypt has reacted, reportedly strengthening air defenses around the Suez Canal.
Still, no matter what happens next, the US-Israel-Iran war has already made Gulf states evaluate defense partnerships with the US. Rather than making them safe, US bases have made them a target.

"There is widespread disappointment across the region with the US over the folly of the war, the erratic nature of Washington's military and diplomatic conduct, and its decision to prioritize Israel's defense over that of its Gulf partners," Hasan Alhasan, a senior fellow at the IISS, told news agency Bloomberg this week. "If the US liberation of Kuwait in 1991 was the moment that established America's role in the region, the 2026 war may be remembered as the moment that undid it."
Gulf states are widening their outreach with, for example, the UAE getting closer to Israel and the Saudis entering the Mecca defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey.

"The Gulf states have already moved toward strategic autonomy and self-reliance," Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer at the School of Security Studies at King's College London, wrote for online outlet Middle East Eye this week. "A lame-duck Trump will speed that process."
That's even though a Democrat-led Congress might make the US a slightly more reliable partner again.
body_zh: 唐纳德·特朗普总统在其政党本周在美国中期选举中惨败后承认，与伊朗的战争可能是其中的一个原因。
特朗普对福克斯新闻表示：“我认为其中一部分原因是伊朗，但与此同时，人们理解我对伊朗所做的事情的重要性。”他承认美国选民不愿意接受战争对天然气价格的影响。
观察人士称，美国和以色列一直推迟对伊朗发动重大袭击，直到两国都举行了选举。
10月底，《华尔街日报》报道称，特朗普政府已警告海湾国家政府做好中期选举后短暂而激烈的军事行动的准备。
虽然外交政策是美国总统的职权范围，但分析人士指出，民主党控制的国会表面上可能会扣留特朗普军事远征的资金。然而，新当选的民主党政客要到明年初才会就任。
正如两位美国政治学教授本周在《外交事务》杂志上撰文，过去的美国总统，比如特朗普，成为“跛脚鸭”——即失去国会控制权、无法连任的总统——往往会加大国际干预力度。
他们解释说：“当他们思考自己的遗产时，跛脚鸭经常转向外交政策，总统职位的权力使他们能够不受讨厌的国内政治的束缚。”教授们认为，特朗普最有可能采取行动的地方之一是伊朗。
另一方面，特朗普还对多家媒体表示，他“并不急于”再次开始轰炸伊朗。
对于伊朗下一步行动的看法也存在分歧。
伊朗人表示，他们已做好应对任何袭击的准备，高级领导人的言论表明，他们可能愿意打击比以前更广泛的目标。这可能包括区域能源和经济基础设施，甚至海底电信电缆或数据中心。
总部位于华盛顿的中东研究所 (MEI) 高级研究员、伊朗问题专家罗斯·哈里森 (Ross Harrison) 在本周由 MEI 主办的虚拟简报会上表示，如果伊朗认为其领导层面临生存威胁，那么“所有赌注都将落空”。 “我认为（这次）他们在海湾国家的目标会有所不同……所以这实际上取决于这一切如何展开。”
但其他专家认为，伊朗故意在中期选举前向特朗普施压。现在选举已经结束，伊朗人可能更愿意谈判达成和平协议。
所有这些都让海湾国家陷入了困境，这些国家自冲突开始以来一直是伊朗袭击的主要目标。
阿拉伯联合酋长国领导人的外交政策顾问安瓦尔·加尔加什上周末在巴林举行的由国际战略研究所（IISS）主办的麦纳麦对话安全会议上表示：“我们发现自己陷入了一场危机，我们在外交上非常努力地试图避免这场危机。” “我们显然正在寻求政治出口。”
卡塔尔一直试图在美国和伊朗之间进行谈判，但也一直在其机场进行紧急演习。阿联酋人一直在进行类似的演习。沙特阿拉伯正在考虑在两条战线上爆发战争：这个石油资源丰富的国家已经受到邻国也门胡塞民兵的攻击。甚至埃及也做出了反应，据报道加强了苏伊士运河周围的防空。
尽管如此，无论接下来发生什么，美以伊战争已经让海湾国家评估与美国的防务伙伴关系。美国基地非但没有保证他们的安全，反而让他们成为攻击目标。
国际战略研究所高级研究员哈桑·阿尔哈桑本周对彭博社表示：“整个地区对美国普遍感到失望，因为这场战争是愚蠢的，华盛顿的军事和外交行为反复无常，而且美国决定优先考虑以色列的防务而不是海湾伙伴的防务。” “如果说 1991 年美国解放科威特是确立美国在该地区角色的时刻，那么 2026 年的战争可能会被人们铭记为摧毁美国角色的时刻。”
海湾国家正在扩大其影响力，例如，阿联酋与以色列走得更近，沙特与巴基斯坦和土耳其签署了麦加防御协议。
“海湾国家已经走向战略自治和自力更生，”伦敦国王学院安全研究学院高级讲师安德烈亚斯·克里格本周在在线媒体《中东之眼》上写道。 “跛脚鸭特朗普将加速这一进程。”
尽管民主党领导的国会可能会让美国再次成为稍微更可靠的合作伙伴。

title_en: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
title_zh: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
summary: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.
summary_zh: The country's first nationwide elections since 1969 are due next year - a timetable now thrown into doubt.
body_en: Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary.
Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take.
The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year.
Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March.
Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.
But the president insists the reforms are necessary to move Somalia towards fully democratic elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick their representatives.
Somalia last held nationwide direct elections in 1969 and has been wracked by civil war for more than 30 years, with Islamist militant group al-Shabab controlling many rural areas.
Somalia's president: They tried to kill me five times
On Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that the constitutional changes could not be applied retrospectively to the president's current term.
In a separate decision, the court declared the chief justice's dismissal "null and void", accusing the presidency of interfering with judicial independence.
The president appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the position, to replace Ahmed.
The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was intended to achieve a just and transparent judiciary.
But the court rejected that explanation, insisting that the chief justice could only be removed through established constitutional procedures.
Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the court ruling, saying "the country is facing a grave political crisis", calling on Mohamud to embrace a consensus-based approach.

The confrontation escalated on Thursday when former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of deploying security forces to the Supreme Court and attempting to arrest its chief justice.
Khaire accused the president of launching an "assault on the Supreme Court", according to the AFP news agency.
"Somalia stands at a dangerous juncture. The dismantling of our judiciary is a direct threat to the rule of law," he said.
AFP said it could not independently verify the reported security deployment, although photographs circulating in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the court compound.
The rulings have thrown Somalia's electoral timetable into uncertainty.

The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, but opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland reject the timetable.
